food.text: Until the 1980s, Japanese cuisine was not popular in São Paulo outside the Japanese Brazilian community. By the 1990s, Japanese restaurants were found throughout the city, including a type of fast food sushi restaurant called a temakeria that is unique to Brazil.
Brazilian soybean production increased more than 3000% between 1970 and 2005. In 2005 alone, soybean and soybean derivative exports earned over US$9 billion for Brazil.

In 2024, Brazil was the second-biggest grain exporter in the world, with 19% of the international market share. It is also the world's largest exporter of coffee, soybeans, beef, poultry, cane sugar and orange juice.

Data from ABRESI in 2013 showed that São Paulo had 500 to 600 Japanese restaurants, producing 400,000 sushi meals per day. Ishige-san says that Brazil was one of the first foreign countries where Japanese cuisine became popular.

The term segurança alimentar (food security) was first recorded in official terminology in 1986. Brazil established the right to food and nutrition on 25 August 2010, when it adopted the Policy on Food Security and Nutrition (Decree 7.272).
Argentines consumed 233 million litres of beer in 1980 and 1.57 billion in 2007, about 40 litres per person. Beer consumption has outpaced that of wine since 2001.

Japanese immigrants who came to work on Brazilian coffee farms found the food very different. Brazilian rice was soft and not sticky, and lard, corn flour, cassava flour and garlic seemed strange to them. They adapted by pickling local fruits like papaya, and later began making miso and shōyu.

The first meal Japanese migrants ate on Brazilian soil was rice and beans. Brazilian rice was soft and not sticky the way they were used to, and the heavy use of lard, corn flour, cassava flour and garlic also seemed strange to the newly arrived families.

Japanese immigrants missed the preserves that are fundamental to Japanese cuisine, which did not exist in Brazil at that time. They adapted by pickling local fruits like papaya, and later began manufacturing miso and shōyu.
Japanese immigrants brought most of the food items that Brazilians associate with Asian cuisine today. They also introduced large-scale aviaries well into the 20th century.
The Amazon basin and Brazil's drought-ridden northeast are mostly occupied by subsistence farmers. Both regions are increasingly important as exporters of forest products, cocoa and tropical fruits.

Growing beer production and consumption in Argentina has supported beer festivals called Oktoberfests in places with significant German populations, such as Villa General Belgrano in Córdoba. These celebrations copy Munich's Oktoberfest in an Argentine manner and are tourist attractions.

Japanese cuisine was not popular in São Paulo outside the Japanese Brazilian community until the 1980s. By the 1990s, Japanese restaurants were found throughout the city, including the temakeria, a fast food sushi restaurant type unique to Brazil. In 2013, São Paulo had 500 to 600 Japanese restaurants producing 400,000 sushi meals per day.

Early Japanese immigrants ate meals of rice and cod, but did not know how to desalt the cod and first prepared it over hot coals. Over time the high cost of rice led to it being replaced by cookies made of cornmeal, cassava flour and corn to go with coffee.

art.text: MASP's headquarters in São Paulo, a concrete and glass structure finished in 1968 and designed by Lina Bo Bardi, is considered a landmark of the city and a symbol of modern Brazilian architecture. The museum is also one of the most-visited art museums in the world.

Around the end of World War II, Brazilian architecture embraced Modernism, with clean lines and functional form instead of excessive decoration. Oscar Niemeyer, who became one of the world's greatest modernists, began to present a style that was to become Brazil's very own.

Mid-century modern design, marked by clean, simple lines and a lack of embellishment, gained most of its popularity in North America, Brazil and Europe from roughly 1945 to 1970. It appeared in interior design, product design, graphic design, architecture and urban development.

MASP was founded in 1947 by Assis Chateaubriand and Pietro Maria Bardi. It was the first Brazilian museum to display post-World War II art, and it became known for pioneering work in museology and art education.

Lina Bo Bardi wanted to preserve the view of downtown São Paulo, so she designed a building suspended above the ground on four massive concrete columns. This leaves a free area of 74 meters underneath, a construction considered unique worldwide.

MASP holds more than 8,000 pieces, including a European art collection considered one of the finest in Latin America and the Southern Hemisphere. The entire collection was placed on the Brazilian National Heritage list.

Aracy Amaral, born in São Paulo and raised in Buenos Aires, became an art historian who specialized in modernism in Brazil. She focused particularly on her aunt, the painter Tarsila do Amaral, and wrote her doctoral dissertation on Tarsila in 1976.

Aracy Amaral directed the Pinacoteca do Estado de São Paulo from 1975 to 1979 and the University of São Paulo's Museum of Contemporary Art from 1982 to 1986. In 1977 she was appointed a Guggenheim Fellow for a study of international and national influences on Brazilian art.
tags: Pinacoteca do Estado de São Paulo

art.text: MASP built a new annex, the Edifício Pietro Maria Bardi, a 14-story black monolith that opened in March 2025. It cost R$250 million and roughly doubled the exhibition area from 10.485 to 21.863 square meters, replacing the 1954 art-deco Dumont Adams Highrise.

Before becoming a museum director, Aracy Amaral worked as a freelancer for clients including the artists Wesley Duke Lee, Cildo Meireles, Hélio Oiticica and Mira Schendel. She also hosted a radio show on Jovem Pan in 1972.

war.text: During World War II, Brazil was the only South American country to send combat troops overseas. Between September 1944 and May 1945, it deployed 25,700 troops to the Italian front as the Brazilian Expeditionary Force.

Attacks by Axis submarines on Brazilian ships between 1941 and 1944 killed over a thousand people. Thirty-five Brazilian ships were targeted and thirty-two were sunk. The deaths were a key factor in Brazil entering World War II, which until then had stayed neutral.

The Brazilian drug war is an ongoing conflict fought mainly between police militias, drug cartels and federal or state security forces. In 2016, the breakdown of a 20-year truce between the PCC and the Red Command led to a massive uptick in violence across Brazil.

Between August 15 and 19, 1942, the German submarine U-507 sank five coasters and a small boat off the coasts of Bahia and Sergipe, causing 607 casualties, including many women and children. Photographs of the dead on the beaches and survivors' accounts made it clear to Brazilians that the war had reached them. The public was outraged, and Brazil declared war on the Axis on August 22, 1942.

Brazil's main contribution in World War I was at sea. On January 30, 1918, Ministerial Notice No. 501 created the Naval Division for War Operations (DNOG), a fleet that included the Bahia and Rio Grande do Sul, and the dreadnoughts Minas Geraes and São Paulo.

In 1942, US forces established airbases along Brazil's North-Northeast coast. The most notable was at Natal in Rio Grande do Norte, known as the "Trampoline of Victory", which played a crucial role in the Allied war effort before the Operation Torch landing in North Africa in November 1942.

Between 2016 and 2020, a series of gruesome prison riots made headlines worldwide as the PCC fought for control of the North Region against the Família do Norte. On January 1, dozens of PCC prisoners were massacred at the Anísio Jobim Penitentiary Complex in Manaus, and the PCC retaliated with riots in Boa Vista and Natal in the same week. Dismemberments, beheadings and prisoners being burned alive were commonplace in all three riots. In Boa Vista, 33 prisoners were killed, and more than 106 died in those prison riots overall.

The DNOG's war at sea began on August 1, 1918, when the force left the port of Rio de Janeiro. On August 3, German submarine U-43 torpedoed the Brazilian ship Maceió. The fleet reached Freetown in Sierra Leone on August 9 and stayed 14 days, during which crew members began falling ill with Spanish flu. After the fleet anchored at Dakar, the flu hit the crews severely again, killing over a hundred sailors and keeping the Division confined to port for almost two months.

Brazil lost 1,889 soldiers and sailors, 31 merchant ships, three warships and 22 fighter aircraft in World War II. Of the 48 pilots in its 1st Fighter Aviation Group, 22 were killed in action, and the cruiser Bahia sank in 1945 after accidentally detonating its own depth charges in gunnery practice, with 333 casualties. The US bases in Brazil were gradually deactivated in 1944 and 1945, though the US kept a presence on Fernando de Noronha until 1960.

A 1943 American propaganda short called Brazil at War said Brazil planned 3 million conscripts. It was produced by the Office of War Information and the Office of the Coordinator of Inter-American Affairs, and it also highlighted Brazil's rubber and crystal production.

The worst PCC-linked proxy war was fought between Guardiões do Estado and Comando Vermelho, with more than 10,000 killed in gang battles in Ceará state. The Guardiões do Estado displaced hundreds of civilians, burned houses and buses, and carried out massacres and mostly homicides. The most notable atrocity was the Cajazeiras massacre, with 14 killed and 9 injured.

literature.text: Modernism in Brazil is traditionally dated to the Week of Modern Art, held in São Paulo in 1922. It was scheduled to commemorate the centenary of independence and featured poetry recitals, musical concerts and new artistic languages. Many of its intellectuals and artists had lived in Europe after World War I.

Brazilian literature gradually shifted from following Portuguese trends toward an authentic style, searching for truly Brazilian themes and forms. Its most significant literary award is the Camões Prize, shared with the rest of the Portuguese-speaking world. As of 2016, Brazil had eleven recipients.

Cordel literature consists of inexpensive printed booklets of folk novels, poems and songs, sold in Brazilian street markets, mainly in the Northeast. They are named for the strings from which they were traditionally hung for display. Authors called cordelistas recite the verses to win over buyers, accompanied by a instrument called the viola.

Mapuche literature today is made up of an oral tradition and bilingual writings in Spanish and Mapudungun. Notable Mapuche poets include Sebastián Queupul, Pedro Alonzo, Elicura Chihuailaf and Leonel Lienlaf. The Mapuche culture of the sixteenth century had an oral tradition and no writing system; a writing system for Mapudungun was developed since that time.

Oswald de Andrade wrote the Manifesto Antropófago (Cannibal Manifesto) in 1927. In it he argued that Brazil, like a cannibal, should eat foreign culture and, in digestion, create its own culture. Of the 1922 generation, he best represents the rebellious characteristics of the modernist movement.

The 1922 Generation was a nickname for writers including Mário de Andrade, Oswald de Andrade, Manuel Bandeira and Cassiano Ricardo. They combined nationalist tendencies with an interest in European modernism. Mário de Andrade's works included Paulicéia Desvairada and Macunaíma.

Afro-Brazilian literature, as a genre recognizing the writer's ethnic and cultural origins, did not gain national prominence until the 1970s. This followed the revival of Black Consciousness politics known as the Movimento Negro. Earlier writers included Machado de Assis, Cruz e Sousa and Lima Barreto.

Some scholars argue that Recife pioneered Brazilian modernism, despite the official view that São Paulo's 1922 Modern Art Week was the starting point. They point to the poetry of Manuel Bandeira, the sociology of Gilberto Freyre, and popular culture such as frevo and cordel. Recent research shows renewal was under way in several parts of the country.

Oswald de Andrade's text was first published in Correio da Manhã and reprinted in 1924 as the opening of the poetry book Pau-Brasil. It proposed a literature linked to Brazilian reality, based on a rediscovery of the country. It said Brazilian art should be an "export", just like Brazilwood.

In 1980 a group of Paulistanos including Cuti and Oswaldo de Camargo founded an Afro-Brazilian literary group. It is best known for its annual publication Cadernos Negros (Black Notebooks), an anthology of poetry, fiction and essays by Afro-Brazilian writers. Since 1999 it has been coordinated by Esmeralda Ribeiro and Márcio Barbosa.

In 1947 Mário de Andrade's story Frederico Paciência told of a male friendship with homoerotic undertones. Though it did not make the characters' orientation explicit, it was one of the first works to show this attraction in a positive way.

The 1950s brought two classic Brazilian novels with LGBTQ subplots: Gran Sertón: Veredas (1956) by João Guimarães Rosa and Crônica da casa assassinada (1959) by Lúcio Cardoso. They explored spirituality, transvestism, metaphysics and forbidden desire, differently from earlier works.
Vertigem (1926), by Laura Villares, is notorious as the first work written by a Brazilian woman to address lesbianism. It nonetheless gives a moralistic and condemnatory view of its protagonist.

science.text: The Brazilian Academy of Sciences, the national academy of Brazil, was founded on May 3, 1916. It is headquartered in the city of Rio de Janeiro.

Brazil's central agency for science and technology is the Ministry of Science and Technology, which includes the CNPq and Finep. It directly supervises the National Institute for Space Research (INPE), the National Institute of Amazonian Research (INPA) and the National Institute of Technology (INT).

Brazil's economic boom between 2004 and 2012 pushed up spending on research and development. Gross domestic expenditure on R&D almost doubled to PPP$35.5 billion, and between 2004 and 2010 it climbed from 0.97% to 1.16% of GDP.

The Brazilian Academy of Sciences publishes a large number of scientific publications, including the Anais da Academia Brasileira de Ciências, which had an impact factor of 1.280 in 2020. It is also in charge of granting prestigious international awards for outstanding scientific work.
tags: Anais da Academia Brasileira de Ciências

science.text: The Sarney government created the Ministry of Science and Technology in March 1985. Its first head was a person associated with the nationalist ideologies of the past, and although he raised the sector's budget, he stayed isolated in government and had no influence on economic policy.

After the new ministry was created, Brazil's science and technology agencies grew in size but lost some of their former independence and flexibility. They also became more susceptible to patronage politics.
Since 2010, the Brazilian government sector alone has been driving up R&D intensity. The non-government contribution actually declined from 0.57% to 0.52% of GDP by 2012.

The Petrobrás crisis was expected to hit Brazilian research investment hard, because the company alone accounted for about 10% of the country's annual fixed capital investment in recent years. Federal budget cuts and austerity measures announced in 2015 were also expected to affect government R&D spending.

politics.text: Brazil first stayed neutral in World War I to protect its coffee, latex and manufactured exports. After German submarines repeatedly sank Brazilian merchant ships, President Venceslau Brás declared war on the Central Powers in 1917. One such attack, the torpedoing of the steamship Paraná on April 5, 1917, killed three Brazilians. Brazil became the only South American country directly involved in the war.

Brazil declared war on the Axis powers on August 22, 1942, and signed the Declaration by United Nations on February 8, 1943. It sent the Brazilian Expeditionary Force to the Italian Campaign. That made it the only South American country to send combat troops overseas.

Today Brazil is a federation of 26 states and a Federal District, which hosts the capital, Brasília. It is the largest country in South America and the only Portuguese-speaking country in the Americas.

The war declaration of October 1917 did more than answer German attacks. It also served as a means to declare a state of emergency and persecute opponents. Violent repression followed a general strike late in 1917, and anti-war demonstrators, trade unionists, anarchists and pacifists who accused the government of diverting attention from internal problems were among those targeted. Earlier that year, after news of the torpedoing of the Paraná on April 5, 1917 (which killed three Brazilians) arrived, protesters in Porto Alegre raided, looted and torched shops and properties owned by ethnic Germans. On November 1, 1917, a mob in Petropolis damaged German-linked houses, clubs and factories.

Before World War II, Brazil kept strict neutrality and traded with both sides. By 1940 it was Germany's leading export market outside Europe. President Getúlio Vargas, whose administration was ideologically sympathetic to fascism, first hoped to profit by winning favorable trade deals from both sides.

Axis submarine attacks on Brazilian ships between 1941 and 1944 killed over a thousand people and were a key factor in Brazil's entry into the war. Attacks rose sharply after Brazil cut diplomatic relations with the Axis on January 28, 1942. Between August 15 and 19, 1942, U-507 sank five coasters and a small boat off Bahia and Sergipe, with 607 casualties, including many women and children. Photographs of the dead on the beaches and survivors' accounts brought the war home to Brazilians, and Brazil declared war on August 22.

Oscar Niemeyer joined the Brazilian Communist Party in 1945. In 1964 the military removed the government and viewed him as dangerous, ransacking his office. He then left Brazil for good and moved to France to continue his career.

Brazil's neutrality, declared on August 4, 1914, left its economy exposed. Its coffee and latex exports were not seen as essential, and Britain banned coffee imports in 1917 to prioritize vital shipping. Customs duties and export fees fell as the war continued.

In 1942, US forces built airbases along Brazil's North-Northeast coast. The most notable, at Natal in Rio Grande do Norte, was nicknamed the "Trampoline of Victory". The US bases were gradually deactivated in 1944 and 1945, though the US kept a presence on Fernando de Noronha until 1960.

Between September 1944 and May 1945, Brazil deployed 25,700 troops to the Italian front. It lost 1,889 soldiers and sailors, 31 merchant ships, three warships and 22 fighter aircraft. Of the 48 pilots in the 1st Fighter Aviation Group, 22 were killed in action and four more officers died in aviation accidents. The war enhanced Brazil's global prestige and marked its emergence as a significant international power.

Brazil's navy began its war at sea on August 1, 1918, leaving Rio de Janeiro. On August 3, the German submarine U-43 torpedoed the Brazilian ship Maceió. When the fleet reached Freetown in Sierra Leone on August 9, crew members began falling ill with Spanish flu during the pandemic. After the fleet anchored in Dakar, the crews were again severely hit by the Spanish flu, which claimed the lives of over a hundred sailors and kept the Division restricted to port for almost two months.

philosophy.text: Neo-Thomism, the revival of medieval Scholasticism, reached Brazil in the early 20th century. Brazilian Catholic philosophers worked to revitalize the traditional philosophy of Thomism after Scholasticism had almost disappeared by the end of the 18th century.

The Brazilian Institute of Philosophy was founded in São Paulo in 1949 by the jurist and philosopher Miguel Reale. It contributed especially to legal theory, metaphysics, logic, and the philosophy of science.

Julio Cabrera, an Argentine philosopher living in Brazil, is best known for his works on "negative ethics" and on cinema and philosophy. He is a retired professor at the University of Brasília and a former head of its Department of Philosophy.

The Belgian priest Carlos Sentroul co-founded the Neo-Thomist school in Brazil and lectured until 1917, when he returned to Belgium. He favored a moderate approach and asked his audience not to be prejudiced against "our adversaries", calling for the teaching of figures such as Duns Scotus, Comte, and Kant.

The Brazilian Academy of Philosophy, based in Rio de Janeiro, was established in 1989 by a group of Brazilian intellectuals. It aims to promote philosophical creation in Brazil and preserve the country's philosophical heritage through congresses, books, and research support.

Leonardo Van Acker, successor to Carlos Sentroul, championed a critical assessment of Thomism that recognized every philosophical system was subject to errors. His studies were largely devoted to Henri Bergson, and he promoted a philosophical pluralism that sought conciliation between Thomism and modern thought.

In his first book on cinema and philosophy, Julio Cabrera proposed the notion of "logopathy", combining logos (reason) and pathos (feelings). He argued that such cognitive-affective concepts challenge the traditional view of philosophy, which he called apathetic and tied to purely intellectual concepts.

Brazilian scholars translated many Thomistic works into Portuguese. Luís Alberto de Boni published a new 11-volume edition of the Summa Theologica between 1980 and 1981, and later published the Summa contra Gentiles with Odilão Moura in a bilingual format between 1990 and 1996.

culture.text: Samba was one of the first Afro-Brazilian cultural expressions to be admired, taking a privileged position in popular music at the beginning of the 20th century. Afro-Brazilian culture had long been depreciated, but it was revalorized from the 20th century onwards.

Brazil has had no official religion since the first Republican Constitution of 1891, though the Catholic Church stayed politically influential into the 1970s. Brazilian religions are very diversified and inclined to syncretism, and about 90% of Brazilians declared a religious affiliation as of 2004.

Descendants of Lebanese immigrants have shaped Brazilian food. In big towns it is easy to find Lebanese restaurants, and dishes such as sfiha ("esfiha"), hummus, kibbeh ("quibe"), tahina, tabbouleh ("tabule") and halwa are very well known among Brazilians.

Brazil's Catholic share has fallen sharply. The 2022 census indicates that around 57% of Brazilians consider themselves Catholic, down from 90% in 1970. Growth in secularism and Evangelical Protestantism accounts for much of the change.

Under Getúlio Vargas's Estado Novo dictatorship, policies to stimulate nationalism made room for official acceptance of Afro-Brazilian culture. Samba school parades gained government approval through the General Union of Samba Schools of Brazil, founded in 1934.
tags: General Union of Samba Schools of Brazil

culture.text: Capoeira was once considered an activity of criminals and outlaws. In 1953 Mestre Bimba presented it to president Vargas, who called it "the only truly national sport".

Protestants made up fewer than 5% of Brazil's population until the 1960s, but by 2000 they were over 15% of those affiliated with a church. Pentecostal and Charismatic groups account for most of this expansion.

In 1994, about 400,000 people of Ukrainian descent lived in Brazil, and 80% of them lived in a compact region in the south central part of Paraná that they call "Brazilian Ukraine". Prudentópolis has approximately 38,000 Ukrainians, or 75% of the city's population.

Brazil ceased to have an official religion in 1891, when its first Republican Constitution was set forth, and it has remained secular ever since. The Catholic Church nonetheless remained politically influential into the 1970s.

The Frenchman Pierre Fatumbi Verger visited Bahia in 1946 and stayed there until the last day of his life. He photographed the Brazilian people and the nuances of candomblé in black and white, and became part of the religion himself.

In 2003, Law No. 10.639 was signed, requiring Brazilian primary and secondary schools to include the teaching of Afro-Brazilian history and culture in the curriculum. It modified the Law of Guidelines and Bases of Education.

Candomblé, Umbanda and related religions grew from the cults of black slaves shipped from Africa to Brazil, and these cults were persecuted throughout most of Brazilian history, largely because they were believed to be pagan or even satanic. They were legalized only in 1889. Many Umbandists and Candomblers continue to disguise their religion under "Catholic" syncretism, so their numbers could be significantly higher than the official census figure.

This expansion has historically been attributed to American missionaries, entrepreneurs and politicians spreading evangelical theology in South America as a counter to communism, socialism and other movements, including Latin American Catholicism's growing liberation theology.

Seicho-No-Ie, a Japanese new religion, has the largest membership among Japanese new religions in Brazil. In the 1960s it adopted Portuguese as its language of instruction and began advertising itself as a philosophy rather than a religion. By 1988 it had more than 2.4 million members in Brazil, 85% of them not of Japanese ethnicity.
Verger was initiated as a babalawo in Africa and started the Pierre Verger Foundation in Salvador. His entire photographic collection is housed there.
